narrative: In the 2020s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture continued to flourish, building upon the rich heritage of their ancestors. The natural hair movement, which originated in the 1960s and resurged in popularity in the 2000s, remained a powerful force, encouraging individuals to celebrate their afro-textured hair in all its glory. Styles like the Afro, Bantu knots, cornrows, box braids, and locs became increasingly popular, not only as protective styles but also as expressions of identity and community pride. These hairstyles were not just a means of self-expression but also a way to connect with one's heritage and cultural roots. The Jheri curl, although popular in the 1980s and early 1990s, was no longer a dominant force in Black hair culture during this decade. Despite the limited documentation available for this era, it is clear that Black and African women continued to push boundaries and redefine beauty standards, solidifying their place as leaders in the world of hair culture.
